newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone army ordered to crack down on rebels.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone army ordered to crack down on rebels.

text.p: Sierra Leone's government ordered the army and Kamajor traditional hunters on Thursday to flush out rebels it said were attacking civilians, in a further sign that the West African nation's peace deal may be unravelling.

Deputy Defence Minister Samuel Hinga Norman told reporters rebel leader Foday Sankoh was trying to wreck the deal signed in Ivory Coast on November 30 and accused rebel fighters of killing civilians and ambushing vehicles.
He told all Revolutionary United Front rebels to report to four demobilisation camps or face the consequences.

"The government has ordered the army and the Kamajors to attack RUF rebels roaming the country attacking and killing civilians and ambushing vehicles on the highways," Norman, a retired army captain, said.
"We are calling on all RUF fighters to immediately report to the four demobilisation camps set up in the country under the peace agreement or face the consequences."

The rebels accuse the government of infringing the ceasefire by sending Kamajors against their positions. Independent sources say it is unclear whether rebels, former rebels, dissident soldiers or bandit groups are responsible for the attacks.
Military sources say over a dozen soldiers and more than 20 civilians have been killed in attacks or ambushes over the past two weeks.

Sankoh, who took up arms in 1991, has been in Ivory Coast for most of the past year. He signed the peace deal there with President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who took office in March 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule.
Under the peace deal, rebels were supposed to report to demobilisation camps. Officials say that so far, only 30 rebel fighters have reported there.
Officials say plans to send in U.N. peacekeepers have stalled pending agreement from Sankoh.

Norman said that the government was no longer prepared to wait for feedback from Sankoh in Ivory Coast, which brokered the peace deal. The drive against the rebels is codenamed "Operation comb the bush".

"Sankoh is vicious and is betraying the peace process. We are left with no alternative but to flush out RUF fighters so as to protect the lives of civilians which is the government's prime responsibility," Norman added.
There was no immediate comment from Sankoh in Ivory Coast's commercial capital, Abidjan.
But sources with the United Nations, which has been among mediators, say they are still hopeful that the peace deal can be put back on track.
The war has killed an estimated 10,000 people.
